sql_relational_model.prompt: Explain what a primary key and a foreign key are, and why we split data into several tables.
sql_relational_model.prompt_hi: Primary key aur foreign key kya hote hain, aur data ko kai tables mein kyun baanta jaata hai? Apne shabdon mein samjhaiye.

checklist.text: A primary key uniquely identifies each row
A foreign key refers to a key in another table to link rows
Splitting avoids repeating data / keeps each fact in one place

sql_relational_model.reference: A primary key is a column whose value is unique for every row. A foreign key in another table stores that value to point at the row, linking the tables. We split data so each fact is stored once, which avoids inconsistency.
followups: Give an example from customers and orders.

sql_filtering.prompt: A friend writes WHERE city='Lucknow' OR city='Varanasi' AND signup_date > '2025-03-01'. Explain how SQL reads it and how to fix it if they meant both cities after that date.
sql_filtering.prompt_hi: Dost ne likha: WHERE city='Lucknow' OR city='Varanasi' AND signup_date > '2025-03-01'. SQL ise kaise padhta hai, aur dono shehron ke liye date wali condition kaise lagayein?

checklist.text: AND is evaluated before OR
So the date condition only applies to Varanasi
Use brackets around the OR conditions

sql_filtering.reference: AND binds tighter than OR, so the date test applies only to Varanasi and every Lucknow customer is returned. Put brackets around the two city conditions.
followups: What would the corrected WHERE clause look like?

sql_null.prompt: Explain what NULL means in SQL and how you would find customers whose city is missing.
sql_null.prompt_hi: SQL mein NULL ka kya matlab hai, aur jin customers ki city missing hai unhe kaise dhundhenge?

checklist.text: NULL means unknown / missing, not zero or empty text
Comparisons with NULL (including = NULL) are never true / are unknown
Use IS NULL (or IS NOT NULL)

sql_null.reference: NULL means the value is unknown or missing. Any comparison with NULL, even NULL = NULL, is unknown rather than true, so WHERE city = NULL returns nothing. Use WHERE city IS NULL.
followups: What happens to a row with a NULL status when you filter status <> 'delivered'?

sql_aggregates.prompt: What is the difference between COUNT(*) and COUNT(column)? Give an example where they differ.
sql_aggregates.prompt_hi: COUNT(*) aur COUNT(column) mein kya fark hai? Ek example do jahan dono alag result dete hain.

checklist.text: COUNT(*) counts rows
COUNT(column) counts only non-NULL values of that column
Gives a case with NULLs where the counts differ

sql_aggregates.reference: COUNT(*) counts every row. COUNT(column) counts only the rows where that column is not NULL. If 12 orders exist and one has no status, COUNT(*) is 12 but COUNT(status) is 11.
followups: How does AVG treat NULL values?

sql_group_by.prompt: Explain what GROUP BY does. What would `SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM orders` return without it?
sql_group_by.prompt_hi: GROUP BY kya karta hai? `SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM orders` bina GROUP BY ke kya dega?

checklist.text: GROUP BY forms groups of rows with the same value and aggregates per group
One output row per group
Without it the aggregate collapses everything into a single row

sql_group_by.reference: GROUP BY splits rows into groups with the same value and calculates the aggregate for each group, giving one output row per group. Without it the SUM covers the whole table and returns a single row.
followups: Which columns may appear in SELECT next to an aggregate?

sql_having.prompt: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING? Which would you use to find customers with more than one order, and why?
sql_having.prompt_hi: WHERE aur HAVING mein kya fark hai? Ek se zyada orders wale customers dhundhne ke liye kaun sa use karoge aur kyun?

checklist.text: WHERE filters rows before grouping
HAVING filters groups after aggregation
Use HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 because WHERE cannot see aggregates

sql_having.reference: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping, HAVING filters groups after the aggregate has been computed. To find customers with more than one order, group by customer and use HAVING COUNT(*) > 1; WHERE cannot use COUNT.
followups: In what order are WHERE, GROUP BY and HAVING processed?

sql_inner_join.prompt: Explain how an INNER JOIN between customers and orders works, and what goes wrong if you forget the ON condition.
sql_inner_join.prompt_hi: customers aur orders ke beech INNER JOIN kaise kaam karta hai, aur ON condition bhool jaayein to kya hota hai?

checklist.text: Rows are combined where the ON condition matches (customer_id = id)
Rows without a match on either side are not in the result
Without ON every row pairs with every row (cartesian product)

sql_inner_join.reference: An INNER JOIN pairs each order with the customer whose id equals its customer_id, and only matched rows appear. Without an ON condition every order is paired with every customer, giving 12 x 8 = 96 rows.
followups: What would you use if you also needed customers with no orders?

sql_outer_join.prompt: Explain what a LEFT JOIN returns and how it differs from an INNER JOIN. Use customers and orders as the example.
sql_outer_join.prompt_hi: LEFT JOIN kya return karta hai aur INNER JOIN se kaise alag hai? customers aur orders ka example lekar apne shabdon mein samjhaiye.

checklist.text: LEFT JOIN keeps every row from the left table (all customers)
Where there is no match the right-side columns are NULL
INNER JOIN would drop the unmatched (left) rows
A WHERE condition on the right table can remove the NULL rows (put it in ON)

sql_outer_join.reference: A LEFT JOIN keeps every customer; if a customer has no orders, the order columns are NULL. An INNER JOIN returns only customers that have matching orders. A WHERE condition on the orders table would remove the NULL rows, so such conditions go in ON.
followups: How would you list the customers who have never ordered?
What does COUNT(*) return for a customer with no orders after a LEFT JOIN?

sql_multi_table.prompt: Orders have several item rows. Explain what happens to SUM(orders.amount) if you join orders to order_items, and how to avoid it.
sql_multi_table.prompt_hi: Ek order ki kai item rows hoti hain. orders ko order_items se join karke SUM(orders.amount) nikalne par kya hota hai aur ise kaise rokein?

checklist.text: Each order row is repeated once per item row (fan-out)
So the amount is added several times and the total is inflated
Avoid it by not joining items, aggregating before joining, or summing item-level values

sql_multi_table.reference: Joining order_items repeats the order row for each item, so SUM(orders.amount) adds the same amount several times and the total is too large. Avoid by aggregating before the join, not joining items when they are not needed, or summing item-level values.
followups: How can you check how many rows a join produces?

sql_subqueries.prompt: Explain when you would use a subquery, with the example of products priced above the average price.
sql_subqueries.prompt_hi: Subquery kab use karte hain? 'average price se zyada price wale products' ke example se samjhaiye.

checklist.text: A subquery is a query inside another query
The average is computed in a subquery because aggregates cannot be used directly in WHERE
Gives the form WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products)

sql_subqueries.reference: A subquery is a query nested inside another. The average price is computed in a subquery - WHERE price > (SELECT AVG(price) FROM products) - because aggregates cannot be used directly in WHERE.
followups: Why can NOT IN be risky when the subquery returns NULL?

sql_normalization.prompt: Why is it a bad idea to store the customer's name and city on every order row? What would you do instead?
sql_normalization.prompt_hi: Har order row mein customer ka naam aur city store karna kyun galat hai? Uski jagah kya karoge?

checklist.text: The data is duplicated on many rows
It can become inconsistent when the customer's data changes
Store customers in their own table and link with a foreign key

sql_normalization.reference: It duplicates data, so updating a customer's city means changing many rows and some may be missed. Store customers once in their own table and reference them from orders with a foreign key.
followups: How would you model students enrolling in many courses?

sql_indexes.prompt: What is a database index, when does it help, and what is the cost?
sql_indexes.prompt_hi: Database index kya hai, kab madad karta hai, aur uski kya keemat hai?

checklist.text: An extra structure that makes lookups on a column faster
Helps queries that filter, join or sort on that column
Slows writes and uses extra space

sql_indexes.reference: An index is an extra data structure, like a book's index, that makes finding rows by a column fast. It helps queries filtering, joining or sorting on that column, but every insert and update must also update it, and it uses storage.
followups: Should you index every column?

sql_transactions.prompt: Explain what a database transaction is and what ACID stands for, using a bank transfer.
sql_transactions.prompt_hi: Database transaction kya hota hai aur ACID ka matlab kya hai? Bank transfer ke example se samjhaiye.

checklist.text: A transaction is all-or-nothing (atomicity)
Names ACID: atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability
Uncommitted changes are not visible to other sessions (isolation)

sql_transactions.reference: A transaction groups statements so they all succeed or all fail - in a transfer the debit and credit both happen or neither. ACID is atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. Uncommitted changes stay invisible to other sessions.
followups: What does COMMIT do?

http_basics.prompt: Explain how an HTTP request and response work, and the difference between 401 and 403.
http_basics.prompt_hi: HTTP request aur response kaise kaam karte hain, aur 401 tatha 403 mein kya fark hai?

checklist.text: Client sends a method and URL; server replies with a status code and body
401 means not authenticated (missing or invalid credentials)
403 means authenticated but not allowed

http_basics.reference: A client sends a request with a method (GET, POST...) and a URL; the server answers with a status code and usually a body. 401 means the caller is not authenticated; 403 means the caller is known but not allowed.
followups: Why should a GET request never change data?

rest_apis.prompt: Explain the main ideas of a REST API: how URLs and HTTP methods are used, and what idempotent means for PUT.
rest_apis.prompt_hi: REST API ke main idea samjhaiye: URLs aur HTTP methods kaise use hote hain, aur PUT ke liye idempotent ka kya matlab hai?

checklist.text: URLs name resources (nouns)
HTTP methods are the actions (GET read, POST create, PUT replace, DELETE remove)
PUT is idempotent: repeating it leaves the same state, unlike POST

rest_apis.reference: REST uses URLs as nouns for resources and HTTP methods as the actions: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, DELETE removes. PUT is idempotent - repeating it gives the same state - while repeating POST can create duplicates.
followups: Which status code do you return after creating a resource?

api_auth.prompt: What is the difference between authentication and authorisation, and where should API secrets be kept?
api_auth.prompt_hi: Authentication aur authorisation mein kya fark hai, aur API secrets kahan rakhne chahiye?

checklist.text: Authentication proves who you are
Authorisation decides what you may do
Secrets stay on the server, not in front-end code or public repos

api_auth.reference: Authentication verifies who the caller is; authorisation decides what that caller is allowed to do. Secrets such as API keys are kept on the server in environment variables, never in front-end code or public repositories.
followups: What is a JWT?

fastapi_basics.prompt: Explain how FastAPI turns a Python function into an API endpoint, and what Pydantic models are for.
fastapi_basics.prompt_hi: FastAPI ek Python function ko API endpoint kaise banata hai, aur Pydantic models kis kaam aate hain?

checklist.text: A decorator like @app.get('/path') registers the function as the handler
The returned dict/object is sent as JSON
Pydantic models validate and parse request data automatically (422 on bad input)

fastapi_basics.reference: A decorator such as @app.get('/hello') registers the function for that path and method, and the returned value is sent as JSON. Pydantic models validate and parse request bodies automatically and return a 422 error for invalid data.
followups: How would you accept a JSON body with a name and an age?

py_functions.prompt: Explain the difference between printing a value and returning it from a Python function, and what happens if there is no return.
py_functions.prompt_hi: Python function mein value print karna aur return karna kaise alag hai, aur return na ho to kya hota hai?

checklist.text: print only shows text on the screen; the caller cannot use it
return hands a value back to the caller
A function without return gives None

py_functions.reference: print displays text but the caller cannot use it; return hands a value back to the caller. A function without a return statement returns None.
followups: What goes wrong with `def add(x, bucket=[])`?

docker_basics.prompt: Explain what a Docker image and a container are, and how a container differs from a virtual machine.
docker_basics.prompt_hi: Docker image aur container kya hain, aur container virtual machine se kaise alag hai?

checklist.text: An image is a packaged template of code and dependencies
A container is a running instance of an image
Containers share the host kernel; a VM runs its own OS

docker_basics.reference: An image is a packaged template with code and dependencies; a container is a running instance of it. Unlike a virtual machine, containers share the host's kernel, so they are lighter and start faster.
followups: What does a Dockerfile do?

comm_self_intro.prompt: Please introduce yourself. Take about 60 to 90 seconds to tell me who you are, what technical areas you focus on, a key project you've worked on, and why you are interested in this role.
comm_self_intro.prompt_hi: Kripya apna parichay dein. Lagbhag 60 se 90 seconds mein batayein ki aap kaun hain, aapka technical focus kya hai, aapne kaunsa mukhya project banaya hai, aur aap is role mein kyun ruchi rakhte hain.
prompts: Please introduce yourself. Take about 60 to 90 seconds to tell me who you are, what technical areas you focus on, a key project you've worked on, and why you are interested in this role.
Walk me through your background and resume. Highlight what you have built and what kind of engineering challenges excite you.
prompts_hi: Kripya apna parichay dein. Lagbhag 60 se 90 seconds mein batayein ki aap kaun hain, aapka technical focus kya hai, aapne kaunsa mukhya project banaya hai, aur aap is role mein kyun ruchi rakhte hain.
Apne background aur resume ke baare mein batayein. Aapne kya banaya hai aur kis tarah ki engineering challenges aapko pasand hain?

checklist.text: Mentions background, current status, or education
Identifies technical stack or core programming strengths
Highlights a specific project or achievement
Explains motivation for the role or field

comm_self_intro.reference: A strong self-introduction covers: 1) Who you are and current focus, 2) Technical skills and hands-on projects, 3) Tangible outcomes or what you learned, and 4) Why you are passionate about this role.
followups: Which of the projects you mentioned was the most technically challenging and why?

comm_star_story.prompt: Tell me about a time you faced a difficult technical bug or challenge under a tight deadline. How did you resolve it?
comm_star_story.prompt_hi: Kisi aise technical challenge ya bug ke baare mein batayein jo aapne tight deadline mein solve kiya ho. Aapne ise kaise hal kiya?
prompts: Tell me about a time you faced a difficult technical bug or challenge under a tight deadline. How did you resolve it?
Tell me about a time you had a technical disagreement with a peer or teammate. How did you handle it and what was the outcome?
Describe a situation where a project requirement changed late in the timeline. What actions did you take to adapt?
prompts_hi: Kisi aise technical challenge ya bug ke baare mein batayein jo aapne tight deadline mein solve kiya ho. Aapne ise kaise hal kiya?
Kisi aise mauke ke baare mein batayein jab aapka kisi teammate ke saath disagreement hua ho. Aapne use kaise handle kiya?
Aisi situation batayein jab timeline ke aakhri waqt project requirement badal gayi. Aapne kya kiya?

checklist.text: Describes the specific situation or context
Clarifies the specific goal, challenge, or task required
Says what they did (uses 'I', not only 'we') to address the challenge
Shares a concrete result, outcome, or metric from their action
Shares what they learned or how it changed their approach

comm_star_story.reference: Use the STAR method: Situation (set the scene), Task (your goal), Action (what YOU specifically did, using 'I'), Result (measurable outcome), and Reflection (what you learned).
followups: If you had to do that project over again from scratch, what would you do differently?

comm_project_walkthrough.prompt: Walk me through the architecture and design of a key project you built. What was your personal role and what major technical trade-offs did you make?
comm_project_walkthrough.prompt_hi: Apne banaye kisi mukhya project ke architecture aur design ke baare mein batayein. Usme aapka apna role kya tha aur kaun se technical trade-offs aapne kiye?
prompts: Walk me through the architecture and design of a key project you built. What was your personal role and what major technical trade-offs did you make?
Pick your proudest technical project. Explain the high-level architecture, how data flows through it, and the toughest design trade-off you had to make.
prompts_hi: Apne banaye kisi mukhya project ke architecture aur design ke baare mein batayein. Usme aapka apna role kya tha aur kaun se technical trade-offs aapne kiye?
Apne sabse behtar technical project ko chuniye. Uska high-level architecture, data flow, aur sabse mushkil design trade-off samjhaiye.

checklist.text: Explains project purpose and high-level architecture
Clearly articulates their own personal contribution and components built
Discusses technical decisions, alternatives considered, or trade-offs
Describes a significant bug, bottleneck, or hurdle and how it was solved

comm_project_walkthrough.reference: A great project walkthrough covers the system architecture, your specific ownership (what you personally engineered), why you made key tech choices over alternatives, and how you diagnosed and fixed tough bugs.
followups: What was the primary bottleneck or scaling limit of that architecture?
